catalog_quote: 2.2 Stress and Syllable Patterns Word stress is not a salient feature; there is no phonological evidence for its being phonemic. The final syllable in a word is stressed. Intonational contours, however, do play a part in expressing different moods. Unlike many Austronesian languages, the Simberi-Northern Tatau dialect of Mandara has many vowel clusters. Many of these vowel clusters are perceived by the native speakers to fill in a single vowel slot in a syllable. All vowel clusters with the shape: low vowel [e, o, a] + high vowel [i, u] are considered diphthongs, not complex syllable nuclei, ex: ei [eI], ou [ou]. There are four syllable patterns in the language: V, CV, VC, CVC.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final syllable) and as the existing Wikipedia-derived statement, which paraphrases this passage; the primary source is now verified verbatim. Adds that stress is non-salient and non-phonemic and that mood is expressed by intonational contours.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word; it is not phonemic and is described as not salient. Intonation (not stress) carries mood distinctions.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Context: the description is based mainly on the Simberi-Northern Tatau dialect (p. 8); the same page notes that the Big Tabar dialect devoices the vowel of the final syllable of words (sina -> sinA), which the authors do not relate to stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Hong & Hong 2003 describe the language under the name Mandara (= Tabar of Ross 1988, ISO tbf), spoken on Simberi, Tatau, Mapua and Big Tabar islands. Their analysis is 'mainly based on the texts gathered in Simberi-Northern Tatau dialect' (p. 8); the three dialects (Big Tabar, Mapua-Southern Tatau, Simberi-Northern Tatau) are said to differ mainly in vowel shifting, vowel harmony and one or two consonants, and Big Tabar devoices the final-syllable vowel. The stress statement should therefore be read as holding at least for Simberi-Northern Tatau.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: final syllable record (Hong & Hong 2003: 'The final syllable in a word is stressed', stress non-phonemic): the OPD independently confirms 'Stress is not phonemic' and adds post-tonic vowel reduction. It does not state placement, so it neither confirms nor denies 'final' directly; the remark about 'a non-stressed syllable immediately following a stressed syllable' implies stressed non-final syllables occur at least in connected/fast speech, a mild tension with strictly word-final stress but not a competing placement claim. The listing itself shows no dictionary and no further phonology write-up beyond the OPD (whose bibliography cites an unarchived Hong &…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The OPD states only that stress is not phonemic (i.e. predictable, non-contrastive); it gives no placement rule. It adds that vowels reduce to [ɨ]/[ə] or delete in an unstressed syllable right after a stressed one in fast speech. The placement (final syllable) comes from Hong & Hong 2003 p. 9, already held by the project and in the catalog; the OPD is consistent with that but does not itself say where stress falls. The Irrealis paper (#58435) has no stress content (0 hits for stress/accent/tone/intonation/syllable). #32301 Fluckiger & Whaley is about Wandala [mfi] (Chadic 'Mandara', Cameroon), not this language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the OPD or the Irrealis paper.
new_statements.exceptions: None. OPD notes post-tonic vowel weakening/deletion in fast speech and consonant lengthening in repeated open syllables (/lalaro/ [llaro]); Big Tabar dialect pronounces /ts/ as [s].
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is headed 'Mandara (Tabar) (Simberi dialect)'; Hong & Hong 2003 is based mainly on Simberi-Northern Tatau dialect texts. Big Tabar dialect differs phonetically (/ts/ realised [s]; final-syllable vowel devoicing per Hong & Hong 2003 p. 8). SIL record #32301 (Fluckiger & Whaley 1981 'A proposed writing system for the Mandara language') is Wandala [mfi], Chadic, Cameroon, not mand1440, despite appearing in the 2015 tbf listing.
